clue.text: Classically either the rock or the hard place

definitions.text: Classically either the rock or the hard place

parts.words: Classically either the rock or the hard place
parts.note: the modern idiom 'between a rock and a hard place' has a classical forerunner in the Odyssey: a sea monster on a rock facing the whirlpool Charybdis

explanation.surface: A remark that the old cliche about being stuck has a classical original.
explanation.walkthrough: Odysseus had to pass between two hazards in the Strait of Messina, a six-headed monster living on a rock and the whirlpool Charybdis; this is the monster, one half of the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer the monster on the cliff faces the whirlpool, the classical model for any choice between two dangers.

clue.text: Reckon nothing is following in Gibson work

definitions.meaning: to reckon is to tally or calculate a total

definitions.text: nothing is following in Gibson work
definitions.meaning: The word is followed by 'nothing' (zero) in that title

explanation.surface: Someone tallies up and finds nothing comes next in a novel by Gibson.
explanation.walkthrough: William Gibson, the cyberpunk novelist, wrote Count Zero; the answer is the word that 'nothing' (ZERO) follows in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: To reckon is to calculate or tot up; the second reading points to the first word of the title Count Zero.

clue.text: Tail end is (also its lead-in) badly done into the talk of Rome

definitions.text: done into the talk of Rome

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aside about a tail end that has been translated poorly into the language of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' shuffles TAIL END IS; the bracketed '(also its lead-in)' tells you the anagram includes the first word, 'Tail', not just 'end is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A text turned into Latin, the language spoken in ancient Rome, has been rendered in that tongue.

clue.text: Fearful? of stream-of-consciousness writer? Surely not George and Martha

definitions.text: of stream-of-consciousness writer? Surely not George and Martha
definitions.meaning: Edward Albee's play Who's ___ of Virginia Woolf? centres on the warring couple George and Martha; Woolf was a stream-of-consciousness novelist

explanation.surface: A question whether George and Martha could ever be frightened of a modernist novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The second part recalls Albee's title 'Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?': Woolf is the stream-of-consciousness writer, and George and Martha are the play's couple, who are far from cowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fearful means being scared; Albee's title asks who is scared of the novelist Virginia Woolf.

clue.text: Intensive publicity for return of noir from Longfellow

parts.note: hype is intensive promotion or publicity

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word noir is read from its end

explanation.surface: A film-noir revival gets heavy promotion, with a nod to Longfellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noir' looks like film talk, but 'return of' just turns the word round; 'from Longfellow' is the definition, his 1839 prose romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow published a prose romance under this title in 1839, also the name of a Titan of Greek myth.

clue.text: Deep sadness over home in post-war drama

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece written over another sits above it, so the first comes first

parts.note: heartbreak is overwhelming grief or sorrow
a house is a home

explanation.surface: Grief settles over a home in a play from after the war.
explanation.walkthrough: This is George Bernard Shaw's play, published in 1919 just after the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's play of that title appeared just after the First World War, making it a post-war drama.

clue.text: But, -O gods! how do you plague me." (Troilus and Cressida)

definitions.text: But, -O gods! how do you plague me." (Troilus and Cressida)

parts.words: But, -O gods! how do you plague me." (Troilus and Cressida)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap after 'But': in Shakespeare Troilus here addresses the go-between, the uncle of Cressida, by name

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, a lover's cry of exasperation.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Act 1 reads 'But ___, O gods! how do you plague me'; the missing word is the name of Cressida's uncle, the matchmaker the play is famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: Troilus speaks the line to Cressida's uncle, the go-between whose name gave English the verb pander.

clue.text: Sebastiano, Venetian painter, represented in Sir Eric Cilento's private collection

indicators.note: a painter represented in a collection has work inside it, so the name is found inside these words

explanation.surface: A gallery note says a Venetian master is held in a named collector's private hoard.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs across 'siR ERIC CIlento's'; 'represented in' and 'private collection' play on gallery language to point inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sebastiano Ricci was an eighteenth-century Venetian painter of altarpieces and decorative schemes.

clue.text: Work with writer on German home, he pioneered spy genre

indicators.note: in a down entry a piece on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a pen is a writing instrument, a writer
Heim is German for home

explanation.surface: A writer at work in a German house, who invented the spy thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote dozens of popular spy and international-intrigue novels from the 1890s onwards.
explanation.definitionFit: E. Phillips Oppenheim was an early master of the espionage novel, credited with shaping the genre.

clue.text: Haggard character may reveal strange antique RAM

indicators.note: strange means odd or peculiar, so these letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gaunt-looking figure might turn up an odd old ram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' reads as gaunt, but it is H. Rider Haggard, whose hunter Allan is the hero of King Solomon's Mines; 'strange' shuffles ANTIQUE RAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Allan, the big-game hunter of King Solomon's Mines, is H. Rider Haggard's most famous hero.

clue.text: Publisher's cover

parts.note: read as the name of a publisher, Jonathan ___, which is also a sleeveless cloak worn as a cover

explanation.surface: The jacket a publishing house puts on a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' suggests a dust jacket; Jonathan Cape is a London publishing house, and the word is also a garment that covers the shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless cloak covers the shoulders, and the same word names the London publisher Jonathan Cape.

clue.text: Russian is sectarian (and is German, by the way)

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
und is German for and
ist is German for is

explanation.surface: A note that a Russian religious dissenter's name has a German origin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German' tells you to translate 'and is' into German, UND IST; 'by' places them beside ST. The Stundists were a nineteenth-century Russian Protestant sect named from German Stunde, an hour of Bible study.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stundists were a Russian evangelical sect, so one member is a Russian sectarian.

clue.text: Margaret Mahy had them in the family

definitions.text: Margaret Mahy had them in the family

parts.words: Margaret Mahy had them in the family
parts.note: Mahy, the New Zealand children's author, wrote a 1986 novel titled ___ in the Family

explanation.surface: A remark that a children's author had certain relatives at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Mahy's novel 'Aliens in the Family' tells of a girl whose new step-siblings turn out to come from another world.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahy's title puts extraterrestrial visitors inside an ordinary household, beings from another planet.

clue.text: Work that starts off plagiarizing Unfinished Symphony

indicators.note: the starts of these four words are their opening letters, taken in order

explanation.surface: A piece of music that begins by copying Schubert's Unfinished Symphony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the first letters of 'off plagiarizing Unfinished Symphony'; the surface wants 'starts off' as a phrase, but 'off' supplies its own O.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical or literary work is called by the Latin word for work, often numbered in a catalogue.

clue.text: Disadvantage recorded with pride

definitions.meaning: harm or detriment, as in the legal phrase 'without ___'
Jane Austen's novel title pairs Pride with this word

explanation.surface: Something harmful is noted down proudly.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal phrase 'without prejudice' uses the word for harm; 'recorded with pride' points to Austen's Pride and Prejudice.
explanation.definitionFit: Injury or detriment to someone's rights is the legal sense, and Austen set the word beside Pride in her title.

clue.text: Together again in Mamet play

definitions.meaning: brought back together after a separation
David Mamet's short play Reunion shows an estranged father and daughter meeting after many years

explanation.surface: A couple back together in a David Mamet drama.
explanation.walkthrough: David Mamet's 1976 play 'Reunion' has a father and daughter meeting again after twenty years apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Being joined once more after a separation; Mamet's Reunion brings an estranged father and daughter back together.

clue.text: Cast doubt on devil every journalist suggested

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
each means every
ed is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A mischief-maker suggests that every reporter is dubious.
explanation.walkthrough: To impeach evidence or a witness is to question its reliability.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to impeach testimony is to challenge its credibility, so impeached means questioned or discredited.

clue.text: The lands (disputed) of French novelist

indicators.note: lands in dispute are contested and change hands, so these letters change order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Contested territories belonging to a French writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disputed' rearranges THE LANDS into the pen name of Henri Beyle, author of The Red and the Black.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Beyle wrote The Red and the Black and The Charterhouse of Parma under this pen name.

clue.text: No feud shortage in Corelli piece

definitions.text: No feud shortage in Corelli piece

parts.words: No feud shortage in Corelli piece
parts.note: a blood feud is plentiful in a novel by Marie Corelli, whose 1886 book has a word for feud as its title

explanation.surface: A Corelli work is full of quarrels.
explanation.walkthrough: Marie Corelli was a hugely popular Victorian novelist; her 1886 novel 'Vendetta' is a tale of revenge, so a blood feud is in no short supply there. 'Corelli' suggests the composer, but it is the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running blood feud between families, and the title of Marie Corelli's 1886 revenge novel.

clue.text: Show associated with ceremony by Coward

definitions.meaning: Noel Coward's only novel is titled ___ and Circumstance, circumstance being ceremony

explanation.surface: A display linked to formal ritual by a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward's 1960 novel is 'Pomp and Circumstance', where circumstance means ceremonial formality; the phrase is better known from Elgar's marches.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendid ceremonial display, the word paired with circumstance in Coward's novel title.

clue.text: Offered on a plate, and made a good impression

definitions.meaning: an etcher cuts a design into a metal plate, so the image is presented on the plate
an ... plate is inked to print a clear impression; also, something ... is firmly fixed in memory

explanation.surface: Food served up on a dish, and a good impression was made.
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings come from printmaking: the design is cut into a plate, and that plate prints an impression on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Engraving with acid cuts a picture into a metal plate, which then prints a clean impression.

clue.text: Art critic shows resistance to American relative

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance
US stands for American, as in US citizen
kin means relatives, family

explanation.surface: A critic shows hostility towards an American cousin.
explanation.walkthrough: John Ruskin was the leading Victorian art critic, champion of Turner and the Pre-Raphaelites.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ruskin wrote Modern Painters and was the most influential English writer on art of his age.

clue.text: Drink nothing before five in ballet company

parts.note: kir is white wine with blackcurrant liqueur
O is zero, nothing
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Have an aperitif before a ballet performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kirov is the former name of the Mariinsky Ballet of St Petersburg.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kirov was the Soviet-era name of the St Petersburg ballet troupe now called the Mariinsky.

clue.text: Old poet's lady doth show style

parts.note: hath is the old form of has, to have or display a quality
a way, as in 'a way of doing things', is a manner or style

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's wife displays some flair, in old-fashioned language.
explanation.walkthrough: Anne Hathaway married Shakespeare in 1582; 'doth show style' is old-fashioned English for 'has a way' (with her), HATH A WAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Hathaway was the wife of Shakespeare, the poet of an earlier age.

clue.text: Egyptian Zeus beheaded Sir Epicure

indicators.note: a beheaded name loses its head, its opening letter

parts.note: Sir Epicure Mammon is the greedy knight in Ben Jonson's The Alchemist

explanation.surface: An Egyptian god cuts off the head of a gluttonous knight.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Epicure Mammon is the greedy knight in Jonson's The Alchemist; take off the first letter of his surname. Ammon (Amun) was identified by the Greeks with Zeus.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greeks equated the Egyptian chief god Amun with Zeus, worshipping him as Zeus Ammon.

clue.text: Bird comes back in Waterhouse hit

indicators.note: something that comes back travels the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a rail is a marsh bird

explanation.surface: A bird returns in a popular play.
explanation.walkthrough: Keith Waterhouse's hit novel and play 'Billy Liar' has the answer in its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith Waterhouse's Billy Liar names its hero, a fantasist who tells untruths.

clue.text: Swift horses

parts.note: not fast horses but the horses of Jonathan Swift, the rational equine race in Gulliver's Travels

explanation.surface: Racehorses that run fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' reads as fast, but it is Jonathan Swift, whose Gulliver visits a land ruled by wise horses.
explanation.definitionFit: In Gulliver's Travels the noble, rational horses that rule the fourth land are called by this name.

clue.text: Julia had absolute protection

parts.note: in Sheridan's The Rivals the heiress Julia is the ward of Sir Anthony Absolute, so Absolute protected her

explanation.surface: A woman named Julia was completely safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absolute' reads as total, but it is Sir Anthony Absolute in Sheridan's The Rivals, the guardian of Julia; the answer is her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Julia Melville in Sheridan's The Rivals is the ward of Sir Anthony Absolute.

clue.text: Parties not applicable to oracle of Zeus

parts.note: a do is a party, so two of them are do and do

explanation.surface: Celebrations are not relevant to an ancient oracle.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodona in Epirus was the oldest Greek oracle, where Zeus spoke through the rustling of an oak.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodona in northwest Greece housed an ancient shrine where priests read Zeus's will in oak leaves.
